newsitem.title: UK: Genetic lack could cause dangerous vitamin loss.
newsitem.headline: Genetic lack could cause dangerous vitamin loss.

text.p: Up to 15 percent of Britons could have a genetic mutation that makes them deficient in folic acid, an important vitamin, an Irish researcher reported on Friday.
Such people may need more of the vitamin than most others, although researchers said taking 400 micrograms a day, as women are now advised to do, would more than suffice.
"It's the first time that anyone has ever identified a variant that says you must take more of a nutrient," said John Scott at Trinity College in Dublin.

Folic acid is a B-vitamin that, among other things, affects the development of a foetus. Pregnant women have been advised to take folic acid supplements and several governments have considered supplementing common foods like flour with the vitamin.
Babies whose mothers were deficient in folic acid can be born with spina bifida, a deformation of the spine that can cripple and kill.
Scott's group, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health, studied 242 pregnant and 318 non-pregnant women for incidences of a gene known to affect how the body uses folate.

Reporting in the Lancet medical journal, he said women who had two "bad" copies of the gene also had, on average, measurably lower levels of folic acid. Their levels were about 20 percent below normal.
Women with one copy of the mutant gene also had lower levels but only when they were pregnant.
In another study, Scott said he found that babies with spina bifida, and their mothers, were more likely to have the variant gene.
"These results suggest that a substantial minority of people in general populations may have increased folate needs," Scott wrote.

"If genetic variants that cause altered nutrient status are common, as this study suggests, there may be no such thing as a normal' population with respect to nutrient requirements, as was assumed when dietary values were established."

Most current guidelines call for an intake of 200 micrograms a day of folic acid, which is found in green leafy vegetables such as Brussels sprouts, pulses like black-eyed peas and wheat germ. But women of childbearing age are routinely advised to take 400 micrograms.
Scott said any woman who took this amount would be more than covered, even if she had the genetic mutation.
"Four hundred micrograms of folic acid is a lot of folic acid. It would certainly protect them," he said in a telephone interview.
He said people should not rush out and demand to be tested for the gene. "It's a bit premature to talk of testing people as yet because we don't know how much extra they need," he said.
The number of people with the genetic variant differs from country to country. "I think it's 15 percent in the UK and eight percent in Ireland," Scott said.

He said his team would now start looking for other genetic variations that could affect absorption of folates. "Ireland is an ideal place to study genetic diseases because there is very little change in the genetic pool," he said.
